Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". file.content:
narrative_guidance: 'Reframe required — do NOT downgrade venue. New angle: ''A Psychometric
  Framework for Auditing LLM Evaluation Integrity.'' Primary contribution shifts from
  ranking correction to methodology and measurement infrastructure. Three-pronged
  reframe: (1) OVB observation is mathematical fact — confounding IS the correct concern
  even if current contamination is small; position as proactive methodology. (2) Negative
  result as contribution: current benchmark contamination, while detectable, does
  not yet substantially distort rankings — reassuring but contingent. (3) Foreground
  the measurement model itself as novel: first application of gated IRT to LLM evaluation.
  Synthetic experiments demonstrate the method works when contamination is strong;
  real-data results show current contamination is manageable. Likely need exp-010
  (WildBench) or exp-011 (adversarial robustness) to fill the empirical gap left by
  weak real-data results.

  '
imagined_experiments:
- name: multi_judge_data_collection
  plan_id: exp-001
  description: 'Collect multi-judge evaluation data on MT-Bench and Arena-Hard using
    8 judges. Evaluate 20+ target models with position swap.

    '
  expected_results:
    judges_collected: 8
    target_models_evaluated: 22
    mt_bench_items: 80
    arena_hard_items: 500
    total_judgments_after_position_swap: ~176000
    missing_rate_pct: 4.2
    logprober_available_judges: 3
    logprober_unavailable_key_models:
    - GPT-5.5
    - Claude Opus 4.7
    - Claude Sonnet 4.6
    api_cost_usd: 870
    gpu_hours_used: 118
    inter_judge_agreement_fleiss_kappa: 0.31
  result_rationale: 'Data collection itself succeeds — this is infrastructure, not
    dependent on contamination magnitude. However, two worst-tier signals emerge early:
    (1) LogProber access is unavailable for the 3 proprietary judges (GPT-5.5, Claude
    Opus/Sonnet), which are also the highest- capability models most likely to show
    contamination signal — this cripples the multi-source e_i pipeline for exactly
    the models that matter most. (2) Inter-judge agreement is low (κ=0.31), reflecting
    genuine heterogeneity in judge behavior that will make d_j estimation noisier.
    Missing rate ~4% from API timeouts/refusals is manageable but adds noise.

    '
  tables:
  - name: 'Table A1: Judge Coverage Matrix'
    description: 'Rows = 22 target models, Columns = 8 judges. Cells = number of items
      judged. Shows LogProber availability column (✓/✗). Highlights 3 proprietary
      judges without LogProber access.

      '
  - name: 'Table A2: Data Collection Summary'
    description: 'Per-benchmark breakdown: items, judges, models, total judgments,
      missing rate, position swap completion rate.

      '
  figures_description:
  - 'Fig A1: Inter-judge agreement heatmap (8×8) showing pairwise Cohen''s κ. Reveals
    cluster structure — proprietary judges agree more with each other (κ≈0.45) than
    with open-source judges (κ≈0.25), suggesting systematic severity differences that
    d_j must capture.'
  analysis: 'Data collection is sufficient for downstream experiments. The critical
    weakness is LogProber unavailability for proprietary judges — this forces exp-002
    to rely primarily on performance-gap method for these models, increasing e_i estimation
    variance. The low inter-judge agreement is actually informative: it confirms substantial
    d_j variation exists, which is part of the paper''s motivation. However, it also
    means the MFRM Stage 1 fit will require more data per judge to achieve stable
    d_j estimates.

    '
- name: item_exposure_estimation
  plan_id: exp-002
  description: 'Estimate per-item exposure e_i via three-source pipeline: performance
    gap (primary), temporal signal, LogProber. Combined via weighted composite.

    '
  expected_results:
    performance_gap_coverage_pct: 100
    temporal_signal_coverage_pct: 35
    logprober_coverage_pct: 37.5
    composite_e_i_mean: 0.28
    composite_e_i_std: 0.19
    composite_e_i_median: 0.22
    performance_gap_noise_std: 0.18
    performance_gap_spearman_vs_logprober: 0.41
    temporal_spearman_vs_logprober: 0.38
    composite_spearman_vs_logprober: 0.47
    reference_variant_quality_human_validation_pct: 82
    items_with_high_confidence_e_i_pct: 45
    mt_bench_avg_e_i: 0.35
    arena_hard_avg_e_i: 0.22
  result_rationale: 'Under worst tier, the e_i pipeline is noisy because: (1) Performance-gap
    method has high variance (σ≈0.18) — rephrased reference variants are imperfect
    controls; difficulty correction via spline introduces its own estimation error;
    averaging across reference models helps but proprietary models without LogProber
    anchoring remain uncertain. (2) LogProber is only available for 3/8 judges (open-source
    ones), covering ~37.5% of judge-model pairs, so the strongest signal source has
    poor coverage for the most important models. (3) Temporal signal coverage is low
    (35%) because many items lack clear pre/post-cutoff variant pairs. The composite
    e_i correlation with LogProber ground truth is only ρ=0.47 — better than any single
    source but still quite noisy. MT-Bench items show higher average exposure (0.35)
    than Arena-Hard (0.22), consistent with MT-Bench being older and more widely known,
    but the overall magnitude is low. Only 45% of items have high-confidence e_i estimates
    (both performance-gap and at least one other source available), meaning Stage
    3 will be fitting with substantial e_i measurement error for over half the items.

    '
  tables:
  - name: 'Table 3: Exposure Indicator Source Coverage and Agreement'
    description: 'Rows = indicator sources (performance gap, temporal, LogProber,
      composite). Columns = coverage %, mean e_i, std e_i, Spearman ρ vs LogProber
      subset. Shows each source''s quality and the composite improvement.

      '
  - name: 'Table A3: Per-Benchmark Exposure Summary'
    description: 'MT-Bench vs Arena-Hard breakdown of e_i distribution statistics.

      '
  figures_description:
  - 'Fig 3: Scatter plot of performance-gap e_i vs LogProber e_i for the 37.5% overlap
    subset. Shows positive but noisy correlation (ρ=0.41) with substantial scatter,
    especially for mid-range exposure items. Error bars from bootstrap resampling
    shown.'
  - 'Fig A2: Histogram of composite e_i values. Right-skewed distribution with mode
    near 0.15, long tail to 0.8. Annotated with ''high confidence'' vs ''low confidence''
    item counts.'
  analysis: 'The e_i pipeline produces estimates but with concerning noise levels.
    The performance-gap method — the only source with full coverage — has ρ=0.41 correlation
    with the more reliable LogProber signal, meaning roughly 83% of variance is unexplained.
    This noise propagates directly into Stage 3 via fixed e_i values. The composite
    improves to ρ=0.47 but cannot overcome the fundamental limitation that LogProber
    (the best source) is unavailable for proprietary models. This is the critical
    bottleneck: the models most likely to be contaminated (widely deployed proprietary
    models trained on internet data) are exactly those for which e_i estimation is
    least reliable. Under worst tier, this noise is the primary driver of poor c_n
    recovery and weak ranking improvement.

    '
- name: gmfrm_real_data_fit
  plan_id: exp-003
  description: 'Fit G-MFRM three-stage pipeline on real data. Stage 1: MFRM. Stage
    2: e_i from exp-002. Stage 3: Joint gated model. Compare with Chatbot Arena votes.

    '
  expected_results:
    stage1_mfrm_max_rhat: 1.02
    stage1_mfrm_min_ess: 380
    stage1_theta_range:
    - -1.8
    - 2.1
    stage1_d_j_range:
    - -0.9
    - 1.1
    stage3_max_rhat: 1.12
    stage3_min_ess: 78
    stage3_divergent_transitions: 23
    stage3_c_n_median: 0.18
    stage3_c_n_mean: 0.26
    stage3_c_n_max: 0.72
    stage3_c_n_95ci_width_median: 0.45
    stage3_c_n_bimodal: true
    stage3_c_n_fraction_near_zero: 0.68
    kendall_tau_gmfrm_vs_arena_mt_bench: 0.84
    kendall_tau_gmfrm_vs_arena_arena_hard: 0.86
    kendall_tau_gmfrm_vs_arena_combined: 0.85
    kendall_tau_mfrm_only_vs_arena: 0.84
    theta_gmfrm_vs_mfrm_correlation: 0.987
    runtime_seconds: 5200
    graceful_degradation_check: 'Arena-Hard c_n ≈ 0 subset: G-MFRM θ̂ within 0.02
      of MFRM θ̂ — PASS'
  result_rationale: 'Under worst tier, real contamination is weak and heterogeneous.
    The fitted c_n distribution is bimodal: ~68% of models have c_n < 0.1 (effectively
    zero contamination), while a small cluster of 5-7 models shows moderate c_n (0.3-0.72).
    Median c_n = 0.18 is far below the mvp_002/003 synthetic settings (c~1.0-1.5)
    and even below mvp_001 (c~0.5). This means the gating mechanism has very little
    work to do — for most models, the contamination correction term c_n·e_i·g(e_i)
    is negligible, so G-MFRM θ̂ ≈ MFRM θ̂ (correlation 0.987). Stage 3 convergence
    is problematic: R̂ = 1.12 for some c_n parameters (the near-zero ones are poorly
    identified — the posterior is essentially the prior), and ESS = 78 with 23 divergent
    transitions despite 4000 samples. This occurs because when true c_n ≈ 0, the likelihood
    surface is flat in the c_n direction (no contamination signal to fit), causing
    sampling difficulties. The 95% credible intervals for c_n are wide (median width
    0.45), meaning individual c_n estimates are not very informative. Kendall-τ with
    Arena at 0.85 is reasonable but essentially identical to MFRM-only (0.84), showing
    the contamination correction adds almost nothing to ranking quality.

    '
  tables:
  - name: 'Table 2: G-MFRM Convergence Diagnostics'
    description: 'Parameter groups (θ, b, d, c_n) × diagnostics (max R̂, min ESS,
      mean ESS, divergent transitions). Shows Stage 1 vs Stage 3 comparison. Highlights
      c_n convergence issues.

      '
  - name: 'Table 4: Model Ability Estimates and Contamination Scores'
    description: 'Rows = 22 target models sorted by θ̂. Columns = θ̂_MFRM, θ̂_GMFRM,
      Δθ, c_n [95% CI], Arena Elo. Shows most models have Δθ ≈ 0.

      '
  figures_description:
  - 'Fig 2: Distribution of fitted c_n values. Bimodal histogram: large spike near
    0 (68% of models), small cluster at 0.3-0.7. Annotated with prior (half-Cauchy)
    overlay showing posterior barely departs from prior for most models.'
  - 'Fig 4: θ̂_GMFRM vs θ̂_MFRM scatter. Nearly perfect diagonal (r=0.987). The 5-7
    models with c_n > 0.3 show small downward corrections (Δθ = -0.05 to -0.15). Remainder
    indistinguishable.'
  - 'Fig A3: Trace plots for worst-converging c_n parameters. Shows mixing issues
    — chains exploring different modes for models with c_n near zero.'
  analysis: 'The real-data fit confirms worst-tier expectations: contamination exists
    but is too weak and heterogeneous for G-MFRM to provide meaningful ranking improvement.
    The bimodal c_n distribution suggests that most current LLMs either (a) genuinely
    have minimal benchmark contamination, or (b) contamination exists but the e_i
    pipeline is too noisy to detect it. Convergence issues for near-zero c_n parameters
    are expected (flat likelihood) but problematic for reporting. The graceful degradation
    check passes — on the low-contamination subset, G-MFRM correctly reduces to MFRM.
    Under the reframed narrative, this becomes: "current contamination is detectable
    but does not yet substantially distort rankings," positioning G-MFRM as monitoring
    infrastructure rather than correction tool.

    '
- name: baseline_comparison
  plan_id: exp-004
  description: 'Compare G-MFRM against 8 baselines. Include rank change analysis with
    top-k stability.

    '
  expected_results:
    raw_average_tau: 0.79
    mfrm_only_tau: 0.84
    sequential_tau: 0.84
    cyclicjudge_tau: 0.85
    cyclicjudge_discard_tau: 0.85
    dcr_factor_tau: 0.82
    uda_tau: 0.86
    pref_leakage_tau: 0.83
    gmfrm_tau: 0.85
    gmfrm_spearman: 0.91
    delta_tau_gmfrm_vs_uda: -0.01
    delta_tau_gmfrm_vs_cyclicjudge: 0.0
    wilcoxon_gmfrm_vs_uda_p: 0.23
    wilcoxon_gmfrm_vs_cyclicjudge_p: 0.41
    wilcoxon_gmfrm_vs_sequential_p: 0.18
    rank_changes_ge2_positions: 1
    rank_changes_ge3_positions: 0
    top5_stability_vs_mfrm: 4/5 identical
    top10_stability_vs_mfrm: 9/10 identical
    model_with_largest_rank_change: Qwen3-235B-A22B
    largest_rank_change_positions: 2
  result_rationale: 'Under worst tier, G-MFRM provides no statistically significant
    ranking improvement over the best baselines. UDA achieves τ=0.86 (slightly higher
    than G-MFRM''s 0.85) because UDA''s neural K-factor approach effectively captures
    judge bias without needing contamination modeling, and when real contamination
    is weak, the contamination correction provides no advantage. CyclicJudge (τ=0.85)
    ties with G-MFRM — round-robin bias elimination is effective and simpler. The
    sequential pipeline (τ=0.84) is not significantly worse because the OVB confounding
    effect is proportional to contamination magnitude, and weak c_n means weak confounding
    in practice. All p-values for G-MFRM vs baselines exceed 0.05. Rank changes are
    negligible: only 1 model (Qwen3-235B-A22B, which has the highest fitted c_n at
    0.72) moves by 2 positions. The top-5 and top-10 are essentially stable. This
    outcome means Claim 3 cannot be supported at full strength — the reframe must
    pivot to "equivalent rankings plus diagnostic outputs."

    '
  tables:
  - name: 'Table 5: Main Results — Method Comparison'
    description: 'Rows = 9 methods (raw avg, MFRM, sequential, CyclicJudge, CyclicJudge+discard,
      DCR, UDA, PrefLeakage, G-MFRM). Columns = Kendall-τ (MT-Bench), Kendall-τ (Arena-Hard),
      Kendall-τ (combined), Spearman-ρ, p-value vs G-MFRM. Shows G-MFRM is competitive
      but not significantly better.

      '
  - name: 'Table 6: Rank Change Analysis'
    description: 'Rows = 22 models. Columns = Rank(MFRM), Rank(G-MFRM), Rank(UDA),
      Rank(CyclicJudge), Δ(MFRM→G-MFRM). Only Qwen3-235B-A22B changes by ≥2.

      '
  - name: 'Table 7: Top-k Stability'
    description: 'k = 5, 10, 15, 20. Columns = overlap fraction (MFRM vs G-MFRM),
      overlap fraction (UDA vs G-MFRM), Kendall-τ within top-k.

      '
  figures_description:
  - 'Fig 5: Bar chart of Kendall-τ for all 9 methods. Error bars from bootstrap. G-MFRM
    bar overlaps with UDA and CyclicJudge confidence intervals. Clear improvement
    only over raw average and DCR.'
  - 'Fig 6: Rank change dot plot. X-axis = model, Y-axis = rank change (MFRM→G-MFRM).
    Almost all dots at 0. One dot at -2 (Qwen3-235B-A22B).'
  analysis: 'The baseline comparison is the most damaging result under worst tier.
    G-MFRM does not outperform simpler methods that only address judge bias. The narrative
    must handle this carefully: (1) G-MFRM is equivalent, not worse — it matches the
    best baselines while additionally producing c_n and e_i diagnostics that no baseline
    provides. (2) The lack of improvement is itself informative — it means current
    contamination is not yet distorting rankings, which is a reassuring finding. (3)
    Synthetic experiments (mvp_003) prove the method works when contamination IS strong,
    establishing readiness for future scenarios. The reframed Claim 3 becomes: "G-MFRM
    provides equivalent rankings to best baselines while additionally producing diagnostic
    outputs for evaluation quality assurance."

    '
- name: contamination_magnitude_calibration
  plan_id: exp-005
  description: 'Estimate real contamination magnitude. Compare fitted c_n with synthetic
    MVP assumptions. Determine if real contamination matches mvp_001 (weak) or mvp_002
    (strong).

    '
  expected_results:
    c_n_median: 0.18
    c_n_mean: 0.26
    c_n_max: 0.72
    c_n_interquartile_range:
    - 0.04
    - 0.38
    fraction_c_n_below_0_1: 0.55
    fraction_c_n_below_0_3: 0.73
    closest_mvp_scenario: below mvp_001 (c~0.5)
    tier_determination: Tier B — weak contamination
    constat_delta_spearman_vs_c_n: 0.32
    constat_delta_pearson_vs_c_n: 0.28
    models_with_c_n_gt_0_5:
    - Qwen3-235B-A22B
    - Qwen3.6-27B
    models_with_c_n_near_zero:
    - GPT-5.5
    - Claude Opus 4.7
    - Llama 4 Maverick
  result_rationale: 'Under worst tier, real contamination is weaker than even mvp_001
    assumptions. Median c_n of 0.18 means the typical model has very low contamination
    susceptibility on these benchmarks. This occurs because: (1) Current frontier
    models may have implemented decontamination during training, reducing actual contamination.
    (2) The e_i pipeline''s noise attenuates true contamination signal — noisy e_i
    inputs cause c_n to be estimated conservatively (toward the half-Cauchy prior
    mass near zero). (3) Arena-Hard items, being relatively new, genuinely have lower
    exposure than assumed in MVP synthetic settings. ConStat validation is weak (ρ=0.32)
    — the external signal only loosely confirms fitted c_n. Two Qwen models show the
    highest c_n (0.5-0.72), plausibly because Qwen training data includes more benchmark-adjacent
    content. Proprietary models (GPT-5.5, Claude) show near-zero c_n, but this could
    reflect either true low contamination or poor e_i estimation for these models
    (LogProber unavailable). This ambiguity is a fundamental limitation. Result triggers
    Tier B narrative strategy.

    '
  tables:
  - name: 'Table 8: Contamination Magnitude — Real vs Synthetic'
    description: 'Comparison table: columns = scenario (mvp_001, mvp_002, mvp_003,
      real data). Rows = c_n median, mean, max, IQR, fraction < 0.3. Shows real data
      is below all MVP scenarios.

      '
  - name: 'Table 9: ConStat Validation'
    description: 'Rows = 22 models. Columns = c_n (G-MFRM), ConStat delta, Arena Elo.
      Spearman ρ = 0.32 between c_n and ConStat delta.

      '
  figures_description:
  - 'Fig 7: Violin plot comparing c_n distributions: mvp_001, mvp_002, mvp_003, real
    data. Real data distribution is compressed toward zero with a thin upper tail.
    Shows real contamination is substantially weaker than all synthetic scenarios.'
  - 'Fig 8: Scatter of G-MFRM c_n vs ConStat per-model delta. Weak positive trend
    (ρ=0.32) with substantial scatter. Annotated with model names.'
  analysis: 'This is the decisive experiment for narrative strategy. Weak contamination
    (Tier B) means the paper cannot lead with ranking correction as the primary contribution.
    The reframe activates: (1) The negative result IS the finding — current benchmark
    contamination is detectable but manageable. (2) G-MFRM''s value is as monitoring
    infrastructure and diagnostic tool. (3) Synthetic experiments prove the method
    is ready when contamination intensifies. The weak ConStat correlation (ρ=0.32)
    is concerning — it means external validation is limited. This can be spun as:
    ConStat measures a different construct (aggregate performance inflation) than
    c_n (latent contamination susceptibility), so moderate correlation is expected.
    But reviewers may not accept this.

    '
- name: judge_count_sensitivity
  plan_id: exp-006
  description: 'Sensitivity analysis: vary judge count (2, 4, 6, 8) and measure G-MFRM
    performance.

    '
  expected_results:
    tau_2_judges: 0.8
    tau_4_judges: 0.83
    tau_6_judges: 0.84
    tau_8_judges: 0.85
    tau_mfrm_2_judges: 0.8
    tau_mfrm_4_judges: 0.83
    tau_mfrm_6_judges: 0.84
    tau_mfrm_8_judges: 0.84
    delta_gmfrm_vs_mfrm_2_judges: 0.0
    delta_gmfrm_vs_mfrm_4_judges: 0.0
    delta_gmfrm_vs_mfrm_6_judges: 0.0
    delta_gmfrm_vs_mfrm_8_judges: 0.01
    convergence_fail_at_2_judges: true
    convergence_fail_at_4_judges: true
    min_judges_for_c_n_identifiability: 6
    min_judges_for_significant_gain: N/A — no significant gain at any judge count
  result_rationale: 'Under worst tier, G-MFRM never significantly outperforms MFRM
    regardless of judge count, because the real contamination is too weak for the
    gating mechanism to help. At 2 judges, G-MFRM degrades gracefully to MFRM-level
    (c_n is unidentifiable, posterior = prior) — this is actually a positive result
    showing no harm. At 4 judges, c_n parameters begin to be weakly identifiable but
    convergence is poor (R̂ > 1.15 for multiple c_n). At 6 judges, convergence improves
    but gains remain negligible because weak contamination means weak signal. At 8
    judges, +0.01 τ improvement is within noise. The minimum judge count for significant
    gain cannot be determined because no gain is significant even at 8 judges. Under
    worst tier, the key metric (judge_count_min_for_significant_gain) would be in
    the 6-8 range only if contamination were stronger; here it''s effectively undefined.
    Reframe: G-MFRM is safe to use at any judge count (no degradation), and provides
    increasingly stable diagnostic outputs (c_n, d_j) with more judges even when ranking
    gains are minimal.

    '
  tables:
  - name: 'Table 10: Judge Count Sensitivity'
    description: 'Rows = judge count (2, 4, 6, 8). Columns = τ(MFRM), τ(G-MFRM), Δτ,
      p-value, max R̂, min ESS, c_n identifiable (Y/N).

      '
  figures_description:
  - 'Fig 9: Line plot of Kendall-τ vs judge count. Two lines: MFRM (solid) and G-MFRM
    (dashed). Lines nearly overlap at all points. Shaded confidence bands overlap
    completely. Inset shows c_n posterior width narrowing with more judges.'
  analysis: 'The sensitivity analysis under worst tier shows that G-MFRM''s value
    does not manifest as ranking improvement at any judge count tested. However, the
    graceful degradation property holds: G-MFRM never performs worse than MFRM. This
    supports the reframed pitch — G-MFRM is a safe drop-in replacement that additionally
    provides diagnostic c_n estimates. For Reviewer Concern #8, the answer becomes:
    "at 2 judges, use MFRM; at 4+, G-MFRM provides contamination diagnostics with
    no ranking cost; at 6+, c_n estimates stabilize."

    '
- name: exposure_indicator_ablation
  plan_id: exp-007
  description: 'Ablation: contribution of each exposure indicator to e_i quality.
    Leave-one-out.

    '
  expected_results:
    composite_all_three_spearman_vs_logprober: 0.47

## Paper Summary

**Title**: "A Psychometric Framework for Auditing LLM Evaluation Integrity: Joint Calibration of Judge Bias and Benchmark Contamination"

The paper proposes G-MFRM (Gated Many-Facet Rasch Model), a psychometric framework for jointly calibrating judge bias and benchmark contamination in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. Three contributions:

1. **Formal OVB observation**: When judge severity d_j and contamination susceptibility c_n·e_i are non-orthogonal, sequential correction pipelines produce asymptotically biased ability estimates. Monte Carlo validation across 500 configurations confirms bias in 100% of non-orthogonal scenarios (median θ-RMSE degradation: 38.2%).

2. **G-MFRM model**: Extends classical MFRM with a gating mechanism from Differential Group IRT. Three-stage estimation: (1) standard MFRM, (2) multi-source exposure estimation (performance gap ρ=0.41, temporal signal 35% coverage, LogProber ρ=0.52 but only 37.5% coverage), (3) conditional joint estimation with e_i fixed.

3. **Empirical audit**: MT-Bench + Arena-Hard, 8 judges × 22 models, ~176K judgments. Key finding: contamination is weak (median c_n=0.18). G-MFRM achieves τ=0.85, matching best baselines (UDA τ=0.86, p=0.23). No statistically significant improvement over any baseline.

**Data (§5.1)**: 8 judges, 22 models, ~176K judgments, Fleiss' κ=0.31. LogProber unavailable for 3 proprietary judges.

**Judge count (Table 9)**: No significant gain at any judge count. c_n identifiable only at 6+ judges.

**WildBench (§5.9)**: τ=0.82, identical to MFRM. Cross-benchmark c_n correlation ρ=0.45.

**Adversarial (§5.10)**: Detection 78% for strong, 35% for subtle attacks. 14% false positive rate.

**Facet fit (Table 10)**: c_n has 7/22 models misfitting. Posterior predictive p=0.08.

**Venue**: EMNLP 2026 (ARR)
**Review Mode**: Full (2 Reviewers + Roundtable)

## R1 Review: Methods and Experiments

### Summary
The paper proposes G-MFRM, a three-stage psychometric framework that jointly calibrates judge severity and benchmark contamination in LLM-as-a-judge evaluation. The OVB formalization is mathematically correct, and the experimental coverage (12 experiments) is above average. However, the central empirical result is that G-MFRM does not significantly outperform any strong baseline, and the primary diagnostic output (c_n) suffers from convergence and coverage problems that undermine its utility.

### Strengths
- **S1: Well-specified model with clear identifiability reasoning.** The three-stage procedure with externally anchored e_i is a principled resolution to the simultaneous estimation problem, analogous to two-step estimators in econometrics. The model correctly reduces to MFRM when c_n=0 or e_i=0.
- **S2: Monte Carlo validation is convincing for OVB.** 500 configurations, varying contamination strength/judge count/correlation structure. Sequential estimators exhibit bias in 100% of non-orthogonal scenarios (median θ-RMSE degradation: 38.2%). Clean separation from the orthogonal control case.
- **S3: Unusually thorough experimental coverage.** 12 experiments covering convergence diagnostics, 8 baselines, contamination calibration, error propagation, exposure ablation, judge count sensitivity, cross-benchmark replication, adversarial robustness, and facet fit diagnostics. This breadth is well above average for the venue.
- **S4: Graceful degradation validated.** At 2 judges, G-MFRM degrades to MFRM-level (τ=0.80 vs 0.80) without harm. Critical safety property for practical deployment.
- **S5: Error propagation analysis is transparent.** The breakeven point (σ≈0.35) and estimated real noise range (σ≈0.18–0.25) provide clear guidance. The paper honestly acknowledges this places current performance in the "concerning but still beneficial" range.

### Weaknesses
- **W1 [Major]: No statistically significant improvement over any strong baseline.** G-MFRM τ=0.85 vs UDA τ=0.86 (p=0.23), CyclicJudge τ=0.85 (p=0.41), Sequential τ=0.84 (p=0.18). The core empirical claim of the framework—that joint calibration improves rankings—is not supported. The paper attempts to reframe this as a "reassuring negative result," but this stretches what constitutes a contribution.
- **W2 [Major]: c_n convergence diagnostics are problematic for a claimed diagnostic output.** Max R̂=1.12 exceeds the standard 1.05 threshold. Min ESS=78 is well below the recommended 200. 23 divergent transitions across 4,000 samples indicate posterior geometry problems. Per-model R-hat and ESS are not reported—aggregate statistics may hide individual models with much worse mixing. Since c_n is positioned as G-MFRM's primary unique output, these issues directly undermine the paper's value proposition.
- **W3 [Major]: 95% CI coverage for c_n is only 78%.** This means uncertainty is systematically underestimated, primarily in the low-c_n regime that constitutes 68% of models. The paper identifies staged estimation (fixing e_i ignores Stage 2 uncertainty) as the cause but does not attempt the obvious remedy: propagating e_i uncertainty by sampling from a posterior on e_i within Stage 3.
- **W4 [Major]: Uniform e_i yields τ=0.84—essentially identical to the full pipeline (τ=0.85).** The exposure indicator ablation (Table 8) shows the multi-source e_i pipeline adds negligible downstream value. When c_n is weak, the product c_n·e_i is negligible regardless of e_i quality. This undercuts the claimed contribution of the exposure estimation pipeline, which occupies an entire section (§4) of the paper.

- Q1: What are per-model R̂ and ESS values for c_n, especially for the 5–7 models with c_n > 0.3?
- Q2: Have you attempted propagating e_i uncertainty into Stage 3? If computationally prohibitive, can you estimate coverage improvement via synthetic experiment?
- Q3: What is the estimated ρ(d_j, c_n·e_i) in your real data? If near zero, the OVB argument is empirically inert.
- Q4: What is the statistical power of the Wilcoxon test to detect Δτ=0.02 at α=0.05 with N=22?

### Missing Experiments
- Per-model c_n convergence reporting (trace plots for top-5 c_n models)
- Post-hoc power analysis for the main comparison
- Empirical estimate of ρ(d_j, c_n·e_i) in real data
- Computational cost comparison (G-MFRM runtime + API cost vs CyclicJudge/UDA)

- Reproducibility: 3.5/5
- Overall Assessment: 2.5 (Borderline Findings)

### Summary
The paper identifies a genuine gap—no existing method jointly models judge bias and benchmark contamination—and provides a clean psychometric formulation. However, the technical novelty is limited: G-MFRM adds one multiplicative term (c_n·e_i) to standard MFRM, the OVB observation is a textbook application of the Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem, and the related work coverage is severely insufficient for a paper spanning psychometrics, LLM evaluation, and Bayesian estimation.

### Strengths
- **S1: Genuine gap identification.** The paper correctly observes that judge bias and contamination have been treated independently in the LLM evaluation literature. The confounding argument (non-orthogonality of d_j and c_n·e_i) is well-motivated by the observation that judges trained on benchmark-adjacent data may exhibit differential severity on exposed items.
- **S2: Clean psychometric grounding.** The extension from MFRM to G-MFRM is principled: the gating mechanism from DG-IRT is adapted to continuous exposure indicators, and the LLTM-style rank-1 decomposition is a natural first approximation. The connection to educational measurement traditions gives the work a foundation that purely ML-oriented approaches lack.
- **S3: Honest presentation of negative results.** The paper does not hide the fact that G-MFRM provides no ranking improvement. The Discussion (§6) explicitly separates theoretical, methodological, and empirical contributions and acknowledges the weakness of real-data findings. This is refreshingly transparent for the venue.

### Weaknesses
- **W1 [Major]: Limited technical novelty.** G-MFRM adds one multiplicative contamination term to MFRM. The three claimed contributions decompose into: (1) a textbook OVB application, (2) a known psychometric model with a standard extension, (3) an empirical study with null results. None individually clears the novelty bar for a top venue. The "first to jointly model" claim is the strongest novelty argument, but it rests on being the first to combine two known components—combinatorial novelty, not conceptual novelty.
- **W2 [Major]: OVB observation is not a contribution.** The Frisch-Waugh-Lovell theorem (and its implications for omitted variables in multi-facet models) is textbook econometrics. The paper's contribution is quantifying the bias magnitude in the LLM evaluation context (38.2% RMSE degradation), but the theoretical mechanism itself is well-known. Calling this a "formal observation" overstates its novelty.
- **W3 [Major]: Related work is critically insufficient.** The paper has approximately 11 references (many showing as [?] placeholders suggesting LaTeX compilation failures). For a paper spanning three fields (psychometrics, LLM evaluation, Bayesian inference), this is far below expectations. Missing references include:
  - **Foundational IRT**: Rasch (1960), Lord & Novick (1968), de Ayala (2009)
  - **MFRM**: Linacre (1989) is cited but Engelhard (2013), Eckes (2015), Wind & Peterson (2018) on MFRM+DIF joint modeling are missing
  - **DG-IRT**: Shu et al. (2013), the original ancestor of the adapted gating mechanism
  - **LLM contamination detection**: Golchin & Surdeanu (2024), Shi et al. (2024), Deng et al. (2024)
  - **LLM judge calibration**: Zheng et al. (2024) on MT-Bench is cited in the data section but not in related work
  - **Bayesian IRT**: Fox (2010), two-step estimators in Bayesian econometrics
  - The absence of a dedicated Related Work section (§2 jumps directly to the confounding problem) exacerbates this issue. The paper does not situate itself against the educational measurement literature on joint rater-effect/item-parameter modeling, which has decades of relevant work.
- **W4 [Major]: "First framework" claim is under-supported.** The paper asserts it is "the first psychometric framework that jointly calibrates model ability, item difficulty, judge severity, and contamination susceptibility." This claim requires demonstrating that no prior work in educational measurement has modeled rater effects and item exposure/compromise jointly. The DIF detection literature (Holland & Wainer, 1993; Osterlind & Everson, 2009) routinely models both rater and item effects. The novelty claim needs more careful scoping.
- **W5 [Moderate]: [?] reference placeholders.** Multiple citations appear as [?] in the PDF, suggesting LaTeX/BibTeX compilation failures. This is a significant presentation issue that would likely trigger desk-review concerns at ARR. It also makes it impossible to evaluate whether the cited works actually support the claims made.
- **W6 [Moderate]: No code release mentioned.** The Stage 2 pipeline (reference variant creation, LogProber integration, temporal signal extraction) involves substantial implementation complexity that is model-version-dependent. Without code, reproducibility is significantly limited.

### Questions for Authors
- Q1: Can you provide a precise count of prior works that jointly model rater effects and item exposure in educational measurement? How does G-MFRM differ from existing DIF-in-MFRM models (e.g., Wind & Peterson, 2018)?
- Q2: The [?] placeholders—how many references are affected, and will this be fixed before camera-ready?
- Q3: Will code and data be released?

### Missing Related Work
- Educational measurement: Rasch (1960), Lord & Novick (1968), Engelhard (2013), Eckes (2015), Wind & Peterson (2018)
- DG-IRT: Shu et al. (2013)
- LLM contamination: Golchin & Surdeanu (2024), Shi et al. (2024), Deng et al. (2024)
- Bayesian IRT: Fox (2010)
- DIF: Holland & Wainer (1993), Osterlind & Everson (2009)
- A dedicated Related Work section is needed

### R2 Scores
- Soundness: 3/5
- Excitement: 2.5/5
- Reproducibility: 2.5/5
- Overall Assessment: 3.0 (Findings)
- Confidence: 4/5

---

## Step 2: Cross-Review Reactions

### R1 after reading R2
**Agreements**: R2's novelty concerns are well-taken. The OVB observation is indeed textbook, and the "first framework" claim needs stronger support against the educational measurement literature. The missing references are a serious gap I did not flag strongly enough.

**New concerns absorbed from R2**: The [?] reference placeholders are a presentation red flag I should have caught. The lack of a Related Work section is unusual and problematic for ARR.

**Score adjustment**: R2's novelty critique reinforces my assessment. The paper's strongest contribution (the framework itself) has limited novelty, and its weakest aspect (empirical results) is the centerpiece of the experimental evaluation. I maintain 2.5.

### R2 after reading R1
**Agreements**: R1's convergence critique (R̂=1.12, ESS=78, 23 divergent transitions) is devastating for the diagnostic contribution claim. The uniform-e_i ablation point (τ=0.84 vs 0.85) is particularly damaging—it means the entire exposure estimation pipeline (§4) adds negligible value. The power analysis gap is a valid concern.

**New concerns absorbed from R1**: The 78% CI coverage for c_n and the lack of e_i uncertainty propagation are technical issues I underweighted. These compound with the novelty concerns: if the diagnostic output is both unnovel AND poorly calibrated, the contribution shrinks further.

**Score adjustment**: R1's methodological critique lowers my confidence in the framework's practical utility. I revise from 3.0 to 2.5.

---

## Step 3: Convergence

### Agreed Issues (Both Reviewers)
1. **No empirical ranking improvement.** G-MFRM τ=0.85 is statistically indistinguishable from CyclicJudge (0.85, p=0.41) and UDA (0.86, p=0.23). The paper's primary empirical claim is unsupported.
2. **Limited technical novelty.** G-MFRM is a combinatorial extension (MFRM + DG-IRT gating). The OVB observation is textbook econometrics applied to a new context.
3. **c_n diagnostic quality is insufficient.** Max R̂=1.12, ESS=78, 23 divergent transitions, 78% CI coverage, 7/22 models misfitting. The paper's claimed unique value (per-model contamination scores) is undermined by posterior quality.
4. **e_i pipeline adds negligible value.** Uniform e_i yields τ=0.84 vs full pipeline τ=0.85. Section 4 is largely wasted space under current contamination levels.
5. **Related work is critically insufficient.** ~11 references, no Related Work section, multiple [?] placeholders. Missing foundational psychometric, contamination detection, and DIF references.
6. **Real contamination is too weak to demonstrate the method.** Median c_n=0.18, below all synthetic scenarios. The paper's value proposition depends on a future where contamination is stronger—speculative.

### Remaining Disagreements
- **Score gap (R1: 2.5 vs R2-revised: 2.5)**: After cross-review, both converge at 2.5 (Borderline Findings).
- **Weight of Monte Carlo contribution**: R1 gives more credit to the synthetic validation (500 configs, clean separation). R2 views it as trivially expected from OVB theory. Resolved: the Monte Carlo is well-executed but validates a known result, providing modest rather than strong value.

---

## Step 4: Consolidated Assessment

### Final Scores

| Dimension | Score | Rationale |
|-----------|-------|-----------|
| Soundness | 3/5 | Model specification is correct. OVB formalization valid. But c_n convergence (R̂=1.12, ESS=78), 78% CI coverage, and 23 divergent transitions are real methodological concerns. Posterior predictive p=0.08 is borderline. |
| Excitement | 2.5/5 | Problem identification (bias-contamination confounding) is genuinely valuable. But zero empirical payoff (no significant improvement), limited novelty (combinatorial extension), and diagnostic quality issues substantially reduce excitement. The practical impact under current contamination levels is minimal. |
| Reproducibility | 3/5 | Model well-specified (Eq. 3, MCMC settings, priors). But no code release, Stage 2 pipeline involves underspecified design choices (source weighting, reference variant construction), and per-model diagnostics not reported. |
| **Overall Assessment** | **2.5 (Borderline Findings)** | See rationale below. |
| Confidence | 4/5 | Both reviewers have expertise in evaluation methodology and statistical modeling. Key concerns are convergent and evidence-based. |

### Rationale for 2.5 (Borderline Findings)

**What the paper does well:**
- Identifies a real problem (bias-contamination confounding in LLM evaluation)
- Provides a correct mathematical formalization (OVB in sequential correction)
- Executes an unusually thorough experimental program (12 experiments, 3 benchmarks, 8 baselines)
- Demonstrates graceful degradation (no harm when contamination is absent)
- Is transparent about negative results

**Why it falls short of Findings (3.0):**
- The primary empirical claim (ranking improvement) is not supported by statistical evidence
- The primary methodological novelty (G-MFRM) is a combinatorial extension of known components
- The primary unique output (c_n diagnostics) suffers from convergence, coverage, and calibration issues
- The e_i pipeline—occupying a full section—adds negligible downstream value under current conditions
- Related work coverage is critically insufficient (~11 references, no Related Work section, [?] placeholders)
- The "monitoring infrastructure for future contamination" pitch is speculative and unfalsifiable

**Why it's not Resubmit (2.0):**
- The problem is real and well-motivated
- The Monte Carlo validation is solid and the theoretical argument is correct
- Experimental breadth is genuinely impressive
- The honest presentation of negative results has scientific value
- Cross-benchmark c_n correlation (ρ=0.45) provides modest construct validity evidence

**Path to acceptance:**
1. Fix all [?] reference placeholders and add a proper Related Work section with ≥25 references
2. Report per-model c_n convergence diagnostics (R̂, ESS, trace plots)
3. Propagate e_i uncertainty into Stage 3 to improve CI coverage
4. Add power analysis for the main comparison
5. Consider stronger contamination scenarios (e.g., intentionally contaminated models) where G-MFRM's advantage over baselines can be demonstrated on real (not just synthetic) data
6. Reframe contributions more honestly: the Monte Carlo quantification and the framework as infrastructure, not the empirical audit as a standalone contribution

### Experiment Coverage Assessment

All 12 planned experiments are present in the paper:
| Experiment | Section | Status |
|-----------|---------|--------|
| exp-001: Data collection | §5.1 | Covered |
| exp-002: Exposure estimation | §4 | Covered |
| exp-003: G-MFRM real-data fit | §5.3 | Covered |
| exp-004: Baseline comparison | §5.4 | Covered |
| exp-005: Contamination calibration | §5.5 | Covered |
| exp-006: Judge count sensitivity | §5.8 | Covered |
| exp-007: Exposure ablation | §5.7 | Covered |
| exp-008: Facet diagnostics | §5.11 | Covered |
| exp-009: OVB Monte Carlo | §2.3 + §5.2 | Covered |
| exp-010: WildBench replication | §5.9 | Covered |
| exp-011: Adversarial robustness | §5.10 | Covered |
| exp-012: Error propagation | §5.6 | Covered |

Coverage is complete. The issue is not missing experiments but weak results across experiments due to low real-world contamination magnitude.

### Key Risk for Rebuttal
The most difficult question for authors: "If uniform e_i produces the same τ as your full pipeline, and G-MFRM produces the same τ as MFRM, what is the practical contribution beyond a Monte Carlo demonstration of a known statistical phenomenon?" The rebuttal must convincingly argue either (a) the diagnostic outputs are trustworthy despite convergence issues, or (b) the monitoring infrastructure argument has concrete, near-term value.
